thread.title: Dividend Sensei's Portfolio Update 41: 3 Growing Economic Risks You Need To Be Aware Of

author: Dividend Sensei
title: Dividend Sensei's Portfolio Update 41: 3 Growing Economic Risks You Need To Be Aware Of
text:
(Source: imgflip )
Introduction First, let me be very clear that this is my personal portfolio tailored to my specific financial situation, risk profile, time horizon, and personality traits. I am not recommending anyone mirror this portfolio, which is merely designed to show my unique, rule-based, methodical approach to value-focused, long-term, dividend growth investing.
My situation is unique, as though only 31, I'm already retired (medical retirement from the Army), thus making this portfolio an income-focused retirement one (though in a taxable account). I'm also working full-time (self-employed) and thus have an external source of income to continually add to this portfolio. I do not plan to actually tap the portfolio's income stream for 20-25 years, when I plan to move my family (and help support my parents) to the promised land of my people (retired dividend investors): Sarasota, Florida.
What this portfolio can be used for is investing ideas; however, this portfolio includes high-, low-, as well as medium-risk stocks, so it's up to each individual to do their own individual research and decide which, if any, of my holdings are right for you.
For a detailed explanation of my methodology, please read my introductory article to the EDDGE (Eternal Daily Dividend Growth Experiment) 4.0 portfolio. However, keep in mind that the portfolio is not static, and both it and the underlying investment strategy will evolve and adapt over time. This is because a changing world, new knowledge, and more experience will cause me to fine-tune it over coming years and decades to maximize my income and total returns.
The reason behind owning such a widely diversified portfolio is because I've built this strategy using historical statistical analysis. Statistics requires large sample sizes to have any useful predictive power, and so, the more stocks I own, the more likely the long-term total returns are to approximate the projected returns. As a side benefit, it also creates a highly stable "bunker" portfolio that is likely to easily survive whatever future market storm might come. It also creates a stream of near-daily dividends which will allow me to compound my dividend reinvestment faster.
Note that this experiment has to hit certain performance targets within a fixed time frame:
Break even within 3 years (Kevin O'Leary Principle: If you don't make money after 3 years, it's a hobby, not a business".) Match the market within 4 years. Beat the market within 5 years (on an unlevered basis). Beat smart beta ETFs that have historically outperformed the S&P 500 (like NOBL ) within 6 years. Beat all ETFs or smart beta ETFs (like QQQ ) within 7 years. In case the portfolio fails to hit these targets, then I'll adapt it to add what is outperforming it. That means switching to an alternative plan, which tentatively looks like this:
25% QQQ (Nasdaq ETF, which I consider a superior index to the S&P 500) 25% SCHD (Dividend achiever ETF, which is also superior to the S&P 500) 10% non-dividend stocks (such as Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ), Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ), and Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A , BRK.B )) 5% into bond CEF Guggenheim Strategic Opportunities Fund ( GOF ) - only form of bond exposure I plan on right now 35% individual dividend growth stocks (focused on maximizing long-term total return potential via 20-25 stocks) Also, to make it easier to digest, I've decided to try separating my weekly investment lesson/commentary from the actual portfolio update. This there is no separate commentary because I'm spending time with my family.
Economic Risks Might Be Starting To Show Up In Data When it comes to the long-term health of the US and global economy I'm an optimist. That being said I'm also someone that believes that all investment decisions need to be data driven. One of the promises I made my readers long ago is that when things start to look less rosier on the economic front, I'd let them know. Well things are starting to slow down, especially when it comes to global growth.
(Source: Bloomberg )
Global manufacturing, a proxy for global growth in general, has been falling for about six months. Up until now the US economy has been largely unaffected thanks to the large amount of stimulus created by tax cuts and increased government spending. However, as I'll explain in the recession watch section, US economic growth forecasts are starting to taper off. Here are the three main reasons why I think that might be, and which I'll be watching very closely in the coming months and quarter.
Trade Uncertainties Could Be Weighing On Investment Decisions It was in early February that major trade tensions began, starting with the US threatening to impose 25% and 10% tariffs on global steel and aluminum imports, respectively. With rare exception (China, and Russia mostly), US trade partners were exempt due to a waiver. That ended in May and the result has been tit-for-tax retaliation by various nations against US exports.
(Source: Jeff Miller)
Meanwhile, the trade conflict with China continues to escalate, with earlier trade talks ending in failure. China offered to: increase US imports by $70 billion per year , cut down on patent piracy, and lower non tariff barriers for US companies operating in the country. The US trade rep, under orders from the administration to get an even better deal, instead decided to pull the trigger on the first $50 billion worth of Chinese imports, which face 25% tariffs starting on July 6th ($34 billion worth, with other $16 billion coming soon).
China's retaliation involves a dollar for dollar matching in tariffs. President Trump, incensed by China's inability to meet his terms, has called on US trade representative Robert E. Lighthizer to draw up a list of $200 billion more worth of imports to levy 10% tariffs against. In case China decides to retaliate against that, Trump has warned that any additional countervailing duties from China will be met with yet another $200 billion in tariffed goods (also at 10%). In other words, Trump's game of trade chicken with China has now seen the stakes raised to $450 billion in potential tariffed goods. For context, excluding China, the total US tariff proposals amount to about $50 billion in annual imports. These latest threats, if imposed, would mean that rises 10 fold to $500 billion.
Last week I explained why a full blown trade war is my single biggest concern for the economy. That's because numerous third party studies show that it would likely push the US and global economy into a recession .
According to David Kotok, chief economist with Cumberland Advisors, the increasing risks of a trade war, as well as uncertainty over NAFTA negotiations, are causing major US businesses to pull back on investment .
"You don't invite compromise when you scream at the other guy...What's the policy of the United States? Is it [Peter] Navarro? Is it Mnuchin? Is it Wilbur Ross? Is it Larry Kudlow? Is it the president, who changes his mind back and forth every day? How do you proceed?" - David Kotok
Mr. Kotok and many other economists are pulling back their growth projections as they begin to see rising evidence that US multinationals, which obtain about 40% of revenues from overseas, are tapping the breaks on expansion plans.
(Source: Factset Research)
But here's some good news. Over the past 15 years 65% of new jobs have been created by small businesses. And up until very recently small business optimism has been sky high, especially among manufacturers. For example, according to the National Association of Manufacturers latest survey 95% of manufacturers reported a positive outlook for their companies. That's an all time record for optimism from an organization which lists 90% of its members as small to medium sized businesses. 77% of companies surveyed said they planned to hire more workers over the next year, with 72% saying they plan to increase wages.
So does that mean that smaller businesses, who have less exposure to trade conflicts, might help drive strong job creation and growth? To some extent yes, but small businesses face their own growth challenges.
Rising Input Costs Could Slow Small/Medium Sized Firm Growth While small US focused businesses need not worry about retaliatory tariffs costing them market share overseas, tariffs are still going to impact them via rising input costs. For example, since steel tariffs were announced the price of certain grades of US steel have risen by as much as 39% . Rising steel prices threaten 6.5 million US jobs in the steel consuming manufacturing sector. For context US steel companies employ just 142,000 workers.
But rising steel costs are hardly the end of US based companies' challenges. Energy prices are rising fast, including for key inputs like petrochemicals. Meanwhile, transportation costs are also rising fast mainly due to a massive shortage of truckers.
(Source: Lancaster Colony Investor Presentation)
Due to a large number of truck driver retirements, (plus 94% annual turnover in the industry), there are 63,000 US trucking jobs open right now. That figure is expected to more than double in the coming years. The industry has responded with: increased wages (up to $70,000 per year), signing bonuses ($6,000), and even offering to pay $7,000 to have new drivers obtain commercial driver's license or CDLs (via a 16 week training course). However, it's still not enough because long haul trucking is extremely dangerous (8 times deadlier than being a police officer). Combined with a horrible lifestyle (weeks away from home), this means that even much higher wages and improved benefits means that trucking firms are unable to fill their openings.
Companies like: Amazon ( AMZN ), General Mills ( GIS ), Tyson Foods ( TSN ), and Walmart ( WMT ), are reporting growing delivery delays, and struggling to pass on higher shipping costs to consumers. Walmart has gone so far as to say that rising transportation costs are its single biggest growth headwind right now.
Factor in: higher trucking costs (which touch almost all US goods), rising energy prices, and now tariffs raising input prices even more, and you have a very real risk that small business optimism is about to start falling. That could put an end to all those hirings and wage hikes that small and medium sized businesses were planning on.
Most worrying of all it means that rising inflation (in the face of weaker economic growth) might cause interest rates to rise too high. That would further slow the economy or might even causing an outright recession.
Inflation Is Now At Fed Target But Tariffs And Rising Input Costs Might Lead To Dangerous Rate Hikes The Federal Reserve has a dual mandate to maintain (as best as it can via monetary policy) full employment and stable prices. That means an inflation rate of about 2%. The Fed's preferred metric for inflation is the Personal Consumption Expenditures or PCE index. This is the government's best estimate of how prices are changing for US consumers, and takes substitution effects into account. For example, it assumes that if the price of beef rises but turkey doesn't then consumers will substitute cheaper turkey for more expensive beef.
(Source: Bloomberg)
For most of the last few years PCE was below the Fed's 2% target. And because that target is symmetrical (it's not a ceiling but a long-term target average), the Fed has said it isn't going to slam on the breaks just because inflation is above its target level.
(Source: Bureau Of Economic Analysis )
This is especially true because the Fed is most concerned with what's called Core PCE, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. However, note that in the past three months Core PCE has risen by 0.5% and is now right at the Fed's target level. It's also at the rate that the Fed's current dot plot is forecasting for the end of 2018. In 2019 the Fed estimates that Core PCE will hit 2.1% but then fall back to 2.0% in 2020.
(Source: Federal Open Market Committee)
These are the inflation assumptions that are driving the Fed's current consensus guidance (not a promise just tentative plan). That plan is for two more rate hikes in 2018, three in 2019 and one more in 2020. That would equate to six more rate hikes and bring the Fed funds rate to 3.25% to 3.5%. The Fed assumes that slowing growth beyond 2020 will moderate inflation necessitating one to two rate cuts over the long-term (assuming no recession).
Normally inflation rises due to a strong economy, and so theoretically the Fed should be able to avoid pushing the economy into a recession by hiking rates too aggressively. Because bank prime rates index off the Fed funds rate, the Fed hiking rates increases lending costs for consumers that drive about 70% of US economic growth.
However, the risk here is that while normal inflation is caused by stronger growth tariffs also cause inflation, while simultaneously slowing economic growth. This means that as US trade skirmishes escalate not just might we see greater recession risk due to supply chain disruption and decreased business investment, but the Fed may feel pressure to accelerate its rate hike plan even more. That in turn would almost certainly lead to a yield curve inversion, which 90% of the time in the last 60 years has signalled a recession was coming within 12 to 18 months.
The State Of The Economy (aka Recession Watch) I use five key meta analyses to track the health of the economy. That includes those which have historically proven to be good predictors of recessions: the yield curve, the BaR economic graph, Jeff Miller's meta analysis of leading economic indicators, the St. Louis Fed's smoothed-out recession risk indicator, and the New York and Atlanta Fed's real-time GDP growth tracker.
(Source: Business Insider )
The yield curve has proven the single-most accurate predictor of recessions over the past 80 years. Specifically, when the curve inverts, or goes below 0 (because short-term rates rise above long-term rates), then a recession becomes highly likely. It usually begins within 12-18 months.

(Source: St. Louis Federal Reserve, Ben Carlson)
According to a March 2018 report from the San Francisco Fed, an inverted yield curve has “ correctly signaled all nine recessions since 1955 and had only one false positive, in the mid-1960s, when an inversion was followed by an economic slowdown but not an official recession.” In other words, if the yield curve goes negative there is probably a 90% chance of a recession starting within the next 17 months or so.
Current 2/10 Yield Curve: 0.33% (down from 0.34% last week)
The yield curve is now at its lowest point in 11 years. This is likely due to the stock market falling over trade war concerns. This is creating a flight to safety driving up 10 year bond prices and lowering the 10 year yield. Fortunately, history shows that the actual number isn't significant, and recession risk is low as long as the curve is positive.
Overall, I'm still optimistic that strong economic growth and rising inflation expectations should help to keep long-term rates rising over time and thus put off any potential inversion for many months, if not years. That's especially true if the Federal Reserve avoids hiking short-term rates too aggressively if the curve falls too low.
The second economic indicator I watch is Economic PI's baseline and rate of change, or BaR economic analysis grid. This is another meta analysis incorporating 19 leading indicators that track every aspect of the US economy. That includes the yield curve, through a different version of it.
(Source: Economic PI )
The BaR grid has shown to be a reliable indicator predicting the 1980, 1990, 2001, and 2007 recessions.
With 8 out of 19 economic indicators in the expansion quadrant (indicating accelerating growth), and 11 out of 19 still showing positive (though decelerating) growth, there remains little cause for concern.
(Source: Economic PI)
Note that 11 weeks ago, there were 12 economic indicators in the expansion quadrant. However, the mean coordinate point (economic aggregate) remains about 37% above baseline and showing slight positive acceleration. As long as this remains the case the economy is doing fine and recession risk is low.
Next, there's Jeff Miller's excellent economic indicator snapshot, a rich source of numerous useful market/economic data. It also provides an actual percentage probability estimate for how likely a recession is to start in the next few months.
(Source: Jeff Miller )
What I'm looking at here is the quantitative estimates of short-term recession risks. In this case, the four-month recession risk is about 0.87%, while the probability of a recession starting within nine months is about 24%. While that is up slightly from last quarter, I don't consider it statistically significant. However, I will be watching inflation expectations closely (which drive bond yields) to see if the bond market loses confidence in the country's long-term growth prospects.
For another look at recession risk, I like to use the St. Louis Fed's smoothed-out recession risk indicator. This looks at the risk of a recession beginning in the current month (it's actually delayed two months). It uses a four-month running average of leading economic indicators.
(Source: St. Louis Federal Reserve )
The way to read this graph is to understand that in the past (since 1967), as long as the reading (currently 0.16% recession risk) is under 18%, the economy has never been in a recession. This means that this graph can tell us with about a two-month lead time whether or not the economy is likely to be contracting.
Current Economic Growth Projections Ok, so the economy is nowhere close to a recession right now. But how fast is it growing? Well, we have two models for that, courtesy of the Atlanta Fed and the New York Fed . The actual figure itself is not nearly as important as its trend over the past few weeks and months.
(Source: Atlanta Federal Reserve)
(Source: New York Federal Reserve)
Note that in the past week both forecasts have either dropped precipitously or continued a several-week trend downwards. The New York model has been hit hard by declining manufacturing data which indicates falling orders and shipments. This is evidence that rising transportation costs and or trade related worries might be slowing US economic growth.
These are just models and depending on how they weight different leading indicators, the projections can be wildly different. But they can offer us a reasonable estimate of current economic growth (range of 2.8% to 3.8%). More importantly, the consensus growth estimate (from economists) has been trending up all quarter indicating that US economic growth appears to be not just strong but getting stronger over the last few months. However, with economists now cutting their forecasts due to rising trade conflict fears I'm expecting the consensus figure to start declining soon.
The New York model also is set to estimate future growth and is currently estimating 2.5% growth in Q3 2018 (down from 2.6% last week).
Current growth estimates still bode well for continued job growth, and thus, a continued tightening of the labor market that should eventually boost wages at a faster rate. Last month, private sector wages grew 2.9% YOY, which is up from 2.6% a year ago. Meanwhile, the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates that wage growth is now 2.7% YOY and 2.8% for non-supervisory positions (80% of workers).
That, in turn, could spur stronger consumer spending (70% of the US economy) and drive stronger corporate investment and earnings/cash flow/dividend growth. In fact, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, consumer spending in the last two months grew at 0.5% and 0.6% month over month, respectively. Meanwhile, retail sales for last month came in at 5.9% YOY, which was double what economists were expecting.
Since mid-2015, the overall trend in consumer spending has been positive, which should continue to drive strong growth. However, the risks I cited earlier might start to cause consumer confidence and spending to decline. That's especially true if net job creation starts to decline significantly in the coming months.
Master Watchlist There are about 3,000 dividend-paying stocks in America (including special dividends and variable payers). This list has a goal of eventually listing all low-/medium-risk dividend growth stocks that have the potential to achieve 10+% total return potential.
Target yield indicates approximately fair value, which is the most I'd ever recommending paying for a company, no matter how good it is.
Total return potential is taken from the Gordon Dividend Growth model, which found that over time, total return for dividend stocks tracks yield + long-term dividend growth (a proxy for earnings and cash flow growth).
The projected dividend growth is from either management guidance or the current analyst consensus. Finally, I've included a sector column because some investors, for various reasons, don't want to/can't invest in MLPs.
Bolded and bracketed stocks are at fair value or better and worth buying today. The order of the stocks is the order I recommend buying them in, assuming that maximizing total return is your primary goal.

EQT Midstream was the double down stock the week (to lower cost basis). The purpose of the new stock of the week is to put it on my radar and give me something to double down on if the price were to fall significantly lower.
Plan For The Next Week This week's new stock is Lam Research Corp ( LRCX ), the maker of semiconductor processing equipment used in the fabrication of integrated circuits. Lam began paying a dividend in 2014 and over the past three years has increased its payout by 511% (120% in the last year). However, with a low payout ratio of just 25% and a rock solid balance sheet, Lam can easily sustain a safe and growing dividend despite the cyclical nature of its industry. Over the next decade analysts expect about 19% EPS growth which when combined with the very low payout ratio means that income investors can expect continued strong payout hikes from Lam. With a current yield of 2.6% this fast growing tech stock has the potential to generate about 22% total returns over the next 10 years.
As for my double down stock of the week, I'm once more going back to the EQT Midstream well. That's because it has fallen about 3% since I doubled my position last week. There are four reasons why I think EQM is likely to generate close to 20% total returns over the next decade . The stock is trading at 5.7 times forward cash flow right now due to a large pessimism overhang involving EQT Corp's ( EQT ) midstream reorganization. Because of that valuation EQM is my highest conviction buy and I intend to take advantage of this short-term negativity by doubling down on both EQM and its sponsor, EQT GP Holdings ( EQGP ) in the coming weeks. I'm willing to take both all the way to a 10% stake in my portfolio. EQM gets my cash first due to the depression era valuation.

I use an 11.4% long-term dividend growth estimate and a 2.0% inflation estimate. The 11.4% is the projected long-term dividend growth from the master watchlist, weighted by total return potential, since that is ultimately what my portfolio will end up becoming.
Over time, as I diversify my portfolio, the yield will fall to about 3-4%. But the dividend growth rate should rise to about 9-10%. Ultimately, the goal is to build a highly diversified, low-risk, high-yielding portfolio with strong enough dividend growth to achieve 10-11% inflation-adjusted total returns.
For perspective, the S&P 500's 20-year median annual dividend growth rate has been 6.2% . So, the goal is to about double the market's yield, with about 3-4% faster dividend growth. Bottom Line: Recession Risk Remains Low But Storm Clouds May Be Gathering On The Horizon Please don't misunderstand me. I'm not trying to scare anyone into selling anything. I'm a firm believer in the buy and hold approach to investing and even if I considered us at high recession risk I would still recommend against attempting to time the market.
The purpose of this article is simply to highlight some of the rising economic risks that now appear to be showing up in the data. But remember that while the leading indicators appear to be headed downwards right now, they still point to positive growth. As long as the US economy avoids a recession then: job creation, wage growth, and rising consumer spending, should continue to drive good earnings growth. That in turn means that our portfolio income will continue rising steadily which is ultimately what dividend growth investors need to focus on.
Per a request from some readers, in the next week or two I plan to wargame the next recession which is likely to strike in 2020 or 2021 at the earliest. Specifically, I'll explore the history of US recessions so we can get an idea of how bad things are likely to get. More importantly, I'll highlight the top sectors to buy when recession risks are rising and point out my favorite individual stocks in those sectors.
